weeks.context: You're attacking OWASP Juice Shop — the canonical deliberately-vulnerable web app that EVERY pentester practices on. Your job by Sunday: solve 5 SPECIFIC challenges and write a HackerOne-style report for each. Why these 5? They cover the most common bug classes in real-world bug bounties: XSS, broken auth, IDOR, injection, misconfiguration. Weeks 2-4 expand to 20 more challenges + your first TryHackMe rooms. Project 2 (W5+) moves to HackTheBox real boxes.

days.title: The ethics contract — non-negotiable
days.summary: You only attack what you own or have permission to attack. Sign it today.

items.title: Sign and commit your contract
items.body:
Create repo `vuln-reports`. Create `ETHICS.md` containing:

  # Ethics Contract
  I, [your full name], commit to:
  1. Only test systems I own or have explicit written permission to test.
  2. Report any vulnerabilities I find through responsible disclosure channels.
  3. Never exfiltrate or modify user data beyond minimal proof-of-concept.
  4. Document every test for transparency.

  Signed: [your name]
  Date: [today]

Commit it. Push it. This is the contract you'll uphold for life.

days.title: Set up Kali Linux in a VM
days.summary: Kali in a VM, not bare metal. The right way.

items.title: Boot Kali
items.body: Install VirtualBox (free). Download Kali Linux ISO (kali.org/get-kali/). Create a VM with 4GB RAM, 30GB disk. Install. Boot. Open a terminal. Run `nmap --version`, `sqlmap --version`, `curl --version` — all should work. Take a screenshot of Kali running.

days.title: OWASP Top 10 — the syllabus of web hacking
days.summary: 10 vuln categories cover 90% of real-world breaches.

items.title: One-liner per category
items.body: In `vuln-reports/owasp-notes.md`, write 1 sentence per category explaining what it means in plain English. Example for A03:Injection — 'When user input is treated as code (SQL, OS commands, etc.) instead of as data.'

days.title: Spin up Juice Shop locally
days.summary: Your target for the week. Sandboxed. Safe.

items.title: Run OWASP Juice Shop with Docker
items.creator: various

items.title: Get Juice Shop running
items.body:
Install Docker. Run:
  `docker run --rm -p 3000:3000 bkimminich/juice-shop`
Open http://localhost:3000 in your browser. You should see a fake e-commerce site. Browse it. Open the score board: click the little anchor in the page source HTML (`<a href='#/score-board'>`) — that itself is the first challenge.

days.title: Solve challenges 1, 2, 3
days.summary: XSS + broken auth + score board access.

items.title: Knock out 3
items.body:
Solve these 3 (consult walkthroughs ONLY when fully stuck):
  1. Score Board (find the hidden score-board page)
  2. DOM XSS (perform an XSS via the search box — payload:      `<iframe src="javascript:alert('xss')">` — see what gets reflected)
  3. Login Admin (broken auth — try classic SQLi: `' OR 1=1--`)
Screenshot each success. Save screenshots as `screenshots/01.png`, `02.png`, `03.png`.

items.title: Two more
items.body:
Solve:
  4. View Basket (IDOR — change the userId in the basket request from your      own to another user's; use browser DevTools network tab + replay)
  5. Confidential Document (find a hidden /ftp/ path with leaked docs —      try directory enumeration via gobuster or just guess common paths)
Screenshot success. You now have 5 wins.

days.title: Write the 5 reports — your passport
days.summary: Every report is a HackerOne-style submission. This is what real bounty hunters do.

items.title: How to write a great vulnerability report — HackerOne
Five CVE-style reports
items.body:
In `vuln-reports/reports/`, create 5 markdown files, one per challenge. Format:

  # [Vulnerability name] — Juice Shop
  **Severity:** Low/Medium/High/Critical (with justification)
  **Affected component:** URL + parameter + HTTP method
  **Steps to reproduce:**
    1. ...
    2. ...
  **Impact:** What can an attacker do? (be concrete)
  **Suggested fix:** Specific code or config change
  **Screenshots:** ![POC](../screenshots/01.png)

Update the repo README to list all 5 reports with severity badges.
Tag v0.1.

Pass criteria:
  □ ETHICS.md signed and committed
  □ 5 challenges solved with screenshots
  □ 5 reports written in HackerOne format
  □ README links each report
  □ owasp-notes.md committed

items.title: Could you submit this for real?
items.body: If Juice Shop were a real company on HackerOne, would your XSS report earn a bounty? Your IDOR? What's missing — proof of impact?

weeks.title: Cryptography Essentials — What You Trust and Why
weeks.context: Most crypto attacks aren't on the math — they're on the implementation. This week you understand symmetric vs asymmetric, hashing vs encryption, what's strong vs broken in 2026, and how to spot misuse.
topics: Symmetric encryption — AES-GCM, why GCM beats CBC, what nonces mean
Asymmetric encryption — RSA, ECC; why ECC is preferred for new work
Hashing — SHA-2, SHA-3, BLAKE3; why MD5 and SHA-1 are dead
HMAC vs signatures — message authentication vs non-repudiation
Password hashing — argon2, bcrypt, scrypt — why never SHA-256
Public key infrastructure — certificates, CAs, trust chains
Common crypto mistakes — ECB mode, hardcoded keys, weak randomness
Post-quantum cryptography — the migration timeline, what's coming
tasks: Use openssl to encrypt + decrypt a file with AES-GCM; understand every flag
Generate an RSA keypair; sign + verify a message
Hash a password with bcrypt + argon2; compare workfactor settings
Read about the Heartbleed and Equifax breaches; understand the crypto failures
Run a TLS scan on 3 production sites (yours + 2 banks) with testssl.sh; document weak configs
weeks.project: Build a Crypto Cheat Sheet + Audit Tool. A Python or Go CLI that audits a directory for: hard-coded crypto keys, use of MD5/SHA-1, ECB mode, weak RNG (random.Random vs secrets), short bcrypt rounds. Run it against an open-source codebase you respect; document findings. Commit to GitHub.

weeks.title: Recon and OSINT — Knowing Your Target Without Touching It
weeks.context: Every attack starts with reconnaissance. This week you learn passive (OSINT) and active recon — domain enumeration, port scanning, employee discovery — and you do it ethically (only against authorised targets).

Active recon — port scanning with nmap, service version detection
Web recon — gobuster, ffuf for directory + parameter discovery
OSINT — Maltego, Shodan, Censys, the surfaces nobody thinks about
Employee discovery — LinkedIn scraping, hunter.io for emails
Cloud surface enumeration — exposed S3 buckets, public functions, leaked secrets
Reporting findings — structured + reproducible

weeks.project: Build a Bug-Bounty Recon Pipeline. For a single bug-bounty-eligible target (verify scope first!), a script that runs: subdomain enumeration → liveness check → port scan → directory fuzzing → screenshot every web service. Produces a Markdown report with findings. Test on a HackerOne or Bugcrowd target — strictly within scope.

weeks.title: OWASP Top 10 — The Bugs That Actually Get Found

Vulnerable + outdated components

Each challenge teaches a real vulnerability. Document your solutions in JUICE-SHOP.md. The 'easy' ones take 5 minutes; the 'hard' ones reveal real-world thinking.

weeks.title: Tabletop Exercises and Red Teaming
weeks.context: Red teaming isn't just hacking — it's testing whether your defence catches it. This week you design tabletop exercises and run a mini red-team exercise against your home SOC.
topics: Tabletop exercises — discussion-based simulations
Red team vs pentest vs purple team — the differences
Atomic Red Team — testable detections per MITRE technique
Caldera — automated adversary emulation
Purple team — red + blue collaborating in real-time
Breach + Attack Simulation (BAS) — automated continuous testing
Scoring — what does 'success' mean for a red team engagement?
Communication — preventing the 'security team annoys engineering' problem
tasks: Run 5 Atomic Red Team tests against your home SOC; verify each gets detected
Use Caldera to run an automated adversary emulation
Design a tabletop exercise for one realistic scenario (ransomware in dev)
Run the tabletop with a friend playing the IR commander
Document the gaps it surfaced
weeks.project: Run a Purple Team Exercise. Pick 5 MITRE ATT&CK techniques relevant to your stack. Red side: execute via Atomic Red Team. Blue side: hunt + detect via your Wazuh + Falco. Gap analysis: which techniques were detected, which slipped through, why. Document in PURPLE.md. The output is a prioritised list of detection improvements.

weeks.title: Building a Career in Security — Specialisation + Portfolio
weeks.context: Security is a huge field. You can't be expert at all of it. This week you pick a specialisation, build your portfolio, and start contributing to the community.
topics: Specialisations — AppSec, CloudSec, IR, GRC, Red Team, Detection Engineering
Certifications — OSCP, CISSP, AWS Security Specialty — which matter when
Bug bounty as career signal
OSS contributions — Sigma rules, Atomic Red Team tests, scanner plugins
Writing — blog posts, conference talks, the security Twitter/Mastodon ecosystem
Career paths — consulting vs in-house, startup vs enterprise
Salaries — what to expect, how to negotiate
Mentorship — finding mentors, becoming one
tasks: Pick a specialisation; document why in CAREER.md
Write your first technical security blog post (1500 words)
Contribute one Sigma rule or Atomic Red Team test
Audit your LinkedIn / GitHub / portfolio for security-engineer signals
Reach out to 3 people in your specialisation; ask one short question
weeks.project: Launch Your Security Identity. Pick your specialisation. Write a blog post that demonstrates technical depth. Refresh your portfolio site with security projects from this roadmap. Make 1 OSS contribution. Engage with 5 security people on social. Document the strategy in CAREER.md. The goal: by end of week your name + specialisation are publicly associated.

weeks.title: Capstone — Earn It
weeks.context: The final week. You produce one substantial artifact — bug bounty submission, CVE, full red team report, published research — that proves you operate at security-engineer level.
topics: Picking a capstone — what genuinely demonstrates your skill
Quality over quantity — one deep thing > five shallow
Writing for technical audiences
Responsible disclosure timelines
When to ship vs when to extend
Building a body of work, not just one piece
Continuous improvement after the capstone
The first 90 days of your next security role
tasks: Pick ONE capstone artifact. Don't add scope.
Write the README first — describe the artifact + its impact
Sketch the timeline; deadline is day 7
Talk to one person in the field about the choice
Hard deadline: published + shared by day 7
weeks.project: Pick one of these tracks and complete it to publishable quality: 1) A real bug-bounty submission that's accepted (at least 'low'); 2) A public CVE researched and disclosed responsibly; 3) A full red-team report against a deliberately-vulnerable environment (HTB Pro Labs, OffSec PG); 4) A novel detection rule contributed to Sigma or Atomic Red Team with a writeup; 5) A 3000-word technical research piece published. Whichever you pick — published, public, your name on it.
